source: Zheng et al. (2023) Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in LLMs
finding: Step-back prompting asks the model first to state the general principle behind a problem, then solve it. It is a machine version of Polya's generalise move. On MMLU physics and chemistry it beat chain of thought for PaLM-2L.
numbers: PaLM-2L MMLU Physics 66.4% base, 65.0% CoT, 73.2% Step-Back; Chemistry 70.9% base, 75.3% CoT, 81.8% Step-Back. One exemplar; means over runs with SD.
limits: Authors' own runs. Gain shrinks for the stronger model: GPT-4 Physics 82.9% CoT vs 84.5% Step-Back; Chemistry 85.3% vs 85.6%.
agent_relevance: Abstraction (O2-type restate) as one slot call. Gain shrinks as the base model gets stronger, so test on our model before adopting.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in LLMs
finding: Step-back also helps on knowledge-heavy multi-hop tasks and adds to retrieval.
numbers: PaLM-2L TimeQA 41.5% base, 40.8% CoT, 66.0% Step-Back, 57.4% RAG, 68.7% Step-Back+RAG. GPT-4 TimeQA 45.6%. SituatedQA PaLM-2L 54.3% base, 57.5% Step-Back.
limits: Biggest gain is on a retrieval-style task, not on mathematics. One demonstration was enough; more shots did not help.
agent_relevance: The abstraction call is cheap and separable. A candidate for a code-routed pre-step before attempts.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in LLMs
finding: Error analysis of Step-Back on MMLU Physics: it fixes some baseline errors but breaks others. Most remaining errors are reasoning and maths errors, not abstraction errors.
numbers: Fixes 20.5% of baseline errors and introduces 11.9% new errors (MMLU Physics). Across tasks: fixes up to about 40%, introduces at most about 12%.
limits: Net benefit but real harm. Error categories annotated by the authors.
agent_relevance: Fits G2/G3: an abstraction step needs a downstream check, since about one problem in nine gets worse.

source: Kojima et al. (2022) Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Reasoners
finding: A bare trigger phrase ('Let's think step by step') raises arithmetic accuracy sharply for a large model. It is the baseline that later Polya-style prompts are compared against.
numbers: InstructGPT text-davinci-002: MultiArith 17.7% to 78.7%; GSM8K 10.4% to 40.7%.
limits: Old model, zero-shot only. Gains are far smaller on modern models that already reason by default.
agent_relevance: Do not credit a heuristic prompt with a gain that plain 'think step by step' already gives. Always keep that arm.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Plan-and-Solve Prompting
finding: Plan-and-Solve asks the model to devise a plan, then carry it out. The authors found three failure types in zero-shot CoT on GSM8K: calculation, missing step, and misunderstanding. Planning mostly cuts missing-step errors.
numbers: 46 wrong GSM8K answers from Zero-shot-CoT (GPT-3): calculation 7%, missing step 12%, semantic misunderstanding 27% (shares of the sampled set). Later analysis: Zero-shot-CoT 7/12/27% vs PS+ 5/7/27%.
limits: Small hand-labelled samples; the semantic misunderstanding share did not move.
agent_relevance: A plan call fixes only one error type. Misreading the problem needs a restatement check (O2).

source: Wang et al. (2023) Plan-and-Solve Prompting
finding: Plan-and-Solve gives modest gains over zero-shot CoT on six arithmetic sets.
numbers: text-davinci-003, zero-shot: GSM8K CoT 56.4, PS 57.0, PS+ 59.3; MultiArith 83.8 / 92.2 / 91.8; AQuA 38.9 / 43.9 / 46.0; average 70.4 / 73.5 / 76.7. Few-shot Manual-CoT average 77.6.
limits: GSM8K gain under 3 points; one model, greedy decoding.
agent_relevance: Plan prompts roughly match few-shot CoT. Do not expect a large lift on grade-school maths.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-Most Prompting Enables Complex Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Least-to-most prompting splits a problem into easier subproblems and solves them in order, each using earlier answers. It is the machine form of Polya's 'solve a simpler related problem' and targets easy-to-hard generalisation.
numbers: SCAN length split, code-davinci-002: standard 16.7%, CoT 16.2%, least-to-most 99.7% with 14 exemplars. text-davinci-002: 6.0 / 0.0 / 76.0. code-davinci-001: 0.4 / 0.0 / 60.7. Last-letter concatenation: least-to-most 94.0% at length 4, 74.0% at length 12.
limits: Huge gain on a synthetic symbolic task; much smaller on real maths. Accuracy still falls with length. Old models.
agent_relevance: Ordered decomposition with code passing earlier answers forward fits our design where the program controls flow.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners
finding: Analogical prompting makes the model recall related solved problems, then solve the target. This is Polya's 'do you know a related problem?' as one prompt. It beat 0-shot and few-shot CoT.
numbers: GSM8K: GPT-3.5-turbo 5-shot CoT 75.0%, self-generated exemplars 77.8% (best row); text-davinci-003 14.8% to 61.0%; PaLM2 60.8% to 81.7%. MATH: GPT-3.5-turbo 33.0% to 37.3%; PaLM2 27.1% to 34.8%.
limits: Table row labels were scrambled in text extraction, so row-to-method pairing is partly inferred. Better for large models; retrieved exemplars did better for small ones.
agent_relevance: Recalled analogies can be wrong (next line). Validate with a check, not the model's say-so.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners
finding: Failure analysis of self-generated exemplars: even among correct final answers, recalled problems were often flawed.
numbers: 50 correctly solved problems: 35 exemplars relevant and correct, 9 relevant but with wrong solution, 6 irrelevant. K = 5 exemplars for GSM8K, K = 3 for MATH and BIG-Bench.
limits: 100 problems, hand-labelled by the authors.
agent_relevance: A correct answer does not prove the analogy was good, so do not reward the recall step by final correctness alone.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) SELF-DISCOVER: Large Language Models Self-Compose Reasoning Structures
finding: Self-Discover lets the model pick from a seed list of reasoning modules, adapt them to the task and write a JSON plan. It is a model-chosen heuristic menu, like Polya's list.
numbers: PaLM 2-L zero-shot with Self-Discover: BBH 67%, T4D 69%, MATH 50.5% (200-problem sample). GPT-4 row: BBH 58%, T4D 51%, MATH 70.5%. Beats direct answering on 23 of 25 tasks and CoT on 21 of 25. Claims 10-40x less inference compute than self-consistency style methods.
limits: MATH gain only 1%-7% (2%-3% for GPT-4). 74.7% of MATH failures were computation errors, not wrong structure.
agent_relevance: A model-chosen heuristic menu gives little on maths. Heuristic choice in S6 may be better made by code from check outcomes.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Reverse Thinking Makes LLMs Stronger Reasoners (RevThink)
finding: Training small models on forward reasoning plus a backward question and backward reasoning improved results across 12 datasets. This is a trained form of Polya's 'work backwards' and of checking in the reverse direction.
numbers: Average gain 13.53% over student zero-shot and 6.84% over the best distillation baseline. Mistral-7B average 50.55 zero-shot, 56.08 SKD, 63.23 RevThink; Gemma-7B 46.80 / 54.65 / 61.17. MATH Mistral 10.42 to 15.28; GSM8K 54.71 to 60.88. 10% of data beat full SFT on StrategyQA.
limits: Needs fine-tuning and a teacher (Gemini-1.5-Pro). Maths gains are small compared with Date and TabMWP. At test time the student reasons forward only.
agent_relevance: Shows reversal helps when trained in. Usable without training only as a test-time backward check.

source: Jiang et al. (2024) Forward-Backward Reasoning in LLMs for Mathematical Verification (FOBAR)
finding: FOBAR masks a number in the question, supplies a candidate answer, and asks the model to recover the masked number. That is a literal 'check the result by working backwards' step. Combined with voting it beat self-consistency on six arithmetic sets.
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo average over AddSub, MultiArith, SingleEQ, SVAMP, GSM8K, AQuA: CoT 82.7, Self-Consistency 85.5, Self-Verification 83.2, FOBAR 86.6. GSM8K: CoT 77.2, SC 81.9, FOBAR 85.1. GPT-4 average: CoT 90.6, SC 91.1, FOBAR 91.4. text-davinci-003 (CoT) average: SC 81.4, FOBAR 83.5.
limits: Gain over self-consistency is 0.3 to 1.1 points on average for strong models and zero on some sets. The mask-a-number template works only on numeric word problems.
agent_relevance: Good fit for a code-built backward check on numeric answers (G1, G5): the check is built by code, not judged by the model.

source: Weng et al. (2023) Large Language Models are Better Reasoners with Self-Verification
finding: Backward verification: assume the candidate conclusion, ask the model to recover a condition from the question, and rank candidates by how well it does.
numbers: K = 5 forward candidates, P = 10 backward samples each. Accuracy among problems with disagreeing candidates: GSM8K random 35.7%, CoT 53.4%, verification 58.9%; MultiArith 45.6 / 71.2 / 89.0; AddSub 46.9 / 56.7 / 74.0; SingleEq 43.3 / 51.0 / 74.5. Average gain 2.33% for InstructGPT overall.
limits: Subset rows cover only problems where candidates disagree. Gains smaller on the strongest forward model.
agent_relevance: Backward verification is cheap, and most useful where forward attempts disagree (G3, G4).

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without an outside signal, asking the model to review its own answer does not help and often hurts. With oracle labels it looks strong, which explains why earlier papers overstated gains.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-3.5: 75.9% standard, 75.1% after round 1, 74.7% after round 2 of intrinsic self-correction. CommonSenseQA GPT-3.5: 75.8% to 38.1% (round 1). GPT-4 GSM8K: 95.5% to 91.5% to 89.0% over rounds. GPT-3.5 keeps its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time; when it changes, correct-to-wrong is more likely than wrong-to-correct. Oracle labels lifted GPT-4 GSM8K to 97.5%.
limits: 1,319 GSM8K test problems; two correction rounds; prompts taken from earlier papers.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G1 and G2: Polya's 'look back' needs real output or an independent check, not self-judgment.

source: Petrov et al. (2025) Proof or Bluff? Evaluating LLMs on the 2025 USA Math Olympiad
finding: On six USAMO 2025 proof problems, graded by human experts (7 points each, 42 maximum), eight reasoning models mostly failed.
numbers: Gemini-2.5-Pro 24.4% average over four runs; every other model under 5%. Gemini solved a problem (6/7 or more) in 6 of 24 attempts. Of about 175 solutions from the other models, one earned 7/7.
limits: Six problems, graded within hours of release (low contamination), four runs, double-graded.
agent_relevance: Answer-only benchmarks hide the gap. Use proof-style tasks to test the scaffold.

source: Petrov et al. (2025) Proof or Bluff? Evaluating LLMs on the 2025 USA Math Olympiad
finding: Failure modes: flawed logic, unjustified assumptions, steps called 'trivial', and no change of strategy across attempts. This resembles Schoenfeld's control failure: sticking with one approach.
numbers: Each model often tried the same wrong strategy across all attempts. Flash-Thinking tried several strategies in one run but each only shallowly. Algebra and arithmetic were generally sound (R1 made more arithmetic errors). LLM auto-graders failed to reproduce human grades.
limits: Qualitative categories from judge labels.
agent_relevance: Test code-forced switching of strategy on a stall (S6), since resampling the same prompt does not diversify.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) Cognitive Behaviors that Enable Self-Improving Reasoners
finding: Four named behaviours (verification, backtracking, subgoal setting, backward chaining) decide whether a base model improves under reinforcement learning on Countdown. Qwen-2.5-3B shows them naturally; Llama-3.2-3B does not.
numbers: Countdown after RL: Qwen about 60% accuracy, Llama about 30%. Priming Llama with synthetic traces containing the behaviours lifts it to match or exceed Qwen.
limits: 3B models, one game, a training-time effect rather than prompting.
agent_relevance: These behaviours map onto Polya heuristics (subgoal setting is decomposition, backward chaining is work backwards). Evidence they matter, but as trained-in traits.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) Cognitive Behaviors that Enable Self-Improving Reasoners
finding: What mattered was having the behaviours, not getting the answer right: priming on wrong solutions that contained the behaviours worked about as well as on right ones. Empty chain-of-thought priming gave no gain.
numbers: Incorrect-but-behavioural priming gave performance comparable to correct priming. Empty chain-of-thought control gave no gain and hurt Qwen. Behaviour frequency in 200,000 sampled pretraining documents was classified with Qwen-2.5-32B.
limits: Behaviour counts classified by an LLM; one task family.
agent_relevance: Process form may drive later learning more than answer correctness. Unproven for test-time scaffolds.

source: Cross-paper synthesis of c01-c20 (Zheng, Wang, Yasunaga, Jiang et al.)
finding: Across papers, each single Polya-style prompt gives a few points over plain CoT on maths and more on knowledge or symbolic tasks. Gains shrink as the base model gets stronger.
numbers: GSM8K: PS+ +2.9 over CoT (text-davinci-003); analogical +2.8 over 5-shot CoT (GPT-3.5); FOBAR +3.9 average over CoT (GPT-3.5) but +0.8 for GPT-4. Step-Back on GPT-4 physics +1.6 over CoT.
limits: Different models and baselines; an informal comparison across papers, not a controlled test.
agent_relevance: Expect a few points per heuristic at best. Keep a CoT-only arm and budget tests for small effects.

source: Polya (1945) How to Solve It
finding: Source of the four phases (understand, plan, carry out, look back) and heuristics such as specialise, generalise, analogy, auxiliary problem, and work backwards. All machine prompts above are built from this list.
numbers: No experiments; a taxonomy of moves.
limits: Not opened this session; background knowledge.
agent_relevance: Treat the list as a menu for O1-O5; the control layer matters more than any single heuristic.

source: Schoenfeld (1985) Mathematical Problem Solving
finding: Four factors in problem solving: resources, heuristics, control, belief systems. Protocol analysis found many novices chose one approach early and kept to it, while experts monitored and switched. Teaching the heuristic list alone did not transfer without control training.
numbers: Not verified this session; no figures quoted.
limits: Not opened; recalled from the literature. Human angles are covered by other agents.
agent_relevance: Basis for S6 control: the stall-and-switch rule. Compare with the one-strategy persistence seen in c17.

source: Brown and Walter (1983) The Art of Problem Posing
finding: 'What-if-not' technique: list the attributes of a problem and vary each to pose new problems. Machine counterpart: mutate inputs and conditions.
numbers: Not verified this session.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Fits G3 (test on mutated inputs); a code-driven variation generator could implement it.

source: Search status note for this angle (angle C)
finding: Web search budget and the OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and arXiv query APIs were exhausted or rate-limited this session. Only papers whose arXiv ids were already known were opened. Not found: any direct LLM study of Schoenfeld episodes or Brown-Walter problem posing, and 2025-2026 studies beyond c17-c19.
numbers: Zero queries returned results.
limits: Coverage of 2025-2026 work is thin. A later pass should search for Polya/Schoenfeld-labelled LLM traces, MathArena and proof-grading work, and backward-chaining and specialisation prompts.
agent_relevance: Treat angle C as incomplete for 2025-2026.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) SELF-DISCOVER
finding: Self-composed reasoning structures helped most on a social-reasoning agent task, not on maths.
numbers: T4D: more than 27% absolute gain over baseline for PaLM 2-L (32% for GPT-4) per the paper text. MATH: 1%-7% (PaLM 2-L), 2%-3% (GPT-4).
limits: Gain pairing taken from extracted text; exact baseline arm not re-checked.
agent_relevance: Heuristic structure pays off where the task has hidden structure the model misses; on arithmetic-heavy maths the bottleneck is calculation.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Step-Back Prompting
finding: Ablation: the number of Step-Back demonstrations barely matters, and CoT with or without one shot did little for PaLM-2L on TimeQA.
numbers: TimeQA PaLM-2L: 1-shot 40.7%, CoT 40.8%, CoT 1-shot 38.1%, base 41.5% versus Step-Back 66.0%.
limits: One model family; TDB (take-a-deep-breath) baseline also near base.
agent_relevance: The gain came from the abstraction structure, not from extra reasoning text. A neutral control arm with matched length is needed.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Reverse Thinking (RevThink)
finding: Backward question generation alone already helps, and the full method is sample-efficient.
numbers: With 10% of correct forward reasoning, RevThink beat standard SFT on full data for StrategyQA; gains 4.52% to 7.99% over baselines at 10% data.
limits: Trained student models; Gemini-1.5-Pro teacher.
agent_relevance: Backward questions are informative in themselves; code could generate them as check items.
